q: What is the immediate first-line treatment for acute anaphylaxis, including route, anatomical site, and physiological mechanism of action?
a: Intramuscular (IM) epinephrine 1:1,000 (0.3–0.5 mg in adults) injected into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis). Mechanism: α1 vasoconstriction (reverses hypotension and airway edema) and β2 bronchodilation (relieves bronchospasm and inhibits mast cell mediator release).

q: How does Hereditary Angioedema (HAE) typically present, and what is the single best initial screening laboratory test?
a: Presentation: Recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, non-pitting subcutaneous or submucosal swelling (laryngeal edema, intestinal wall colic) without urticaria or pruritus. Initial screening test: Low serum C4 level (consistently depressed even during asymptomatic remission).

q: What is the underlying molecular defect in Hereditary Angioedema Types 1 and 2, and what key vasoactive plasma mediator drives clinical attacks?
a: Defect: Deficiency (Type 1, ~85%) or dysfunction (Type 2, ~15%) of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH), causing uncontrolled activation of the kallikrein-kinin system. Pathogenic mediator: Bradykinin.

q: How can Acquired C1 Inhibitor Deficiency be laboratory differentiated from Hereditary Angioedema (HAE)?
a: Acquired C1-INH deficiency (seen in older adults with lymphoproliferative disorders or autoantibodies) presents with low C1q levels alongside low C4. Hereditary Angioedema has normal C1q levels.

q: What acute targeted therapies are approved for severe attacks of Hereditary Angioedema, and which class of antihypertensive medications is strictly contraindicated?
a: Acute targeted therapy: C1-INH concentrate, ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor), or icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist). Strictly contraindicated: ACE inhibitors (prevent bradykinin degradation and trigger severe angioedema attacks).

q: What clinical and laboratory findings define Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) in young adults?
a: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections (encapsulated bacteria), chronic diarrhea (Giardia lamblia), and autoimmune cytopenias in patients with markedly decreased serum IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, accompanied by impaired vaccine antibody response.

q: What are the key non-infectious complications of Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID), and what is the mainstay of long-term therapy?
a: Complications: Autoimmune diseases (ITP, AIHA), non-caseating granulomatous organ disease, and a significantly increased risk of Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma. Mainstay treatment: Regular infusions of Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) or Subcutaneous Immunoglobulin (SCIG).

q: What is the clinical significance of Selective IgA Deficiency during blood product transfusions?
a: Patients with total IgA absence (<7 mg/dL) can form anti-IgA antibodies. Transfusion of standard IgA-containing blood products can trigger a severe or fatal anaphylactic transfusion reaction.

q: How must blood components be prepared before administration to a patient with known Selective IgA Deficiency?
a: Provide washed red blood cells or washed platelets (removes residual IgA-containing donor plasma), or use blood products obtained exclusively from IgA-deficient donors.

q: What is the genetic mutation in X-linked Agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's), and what key physical examination finding distinguishes it from CVID?
a: Mutation: BTK gene defect (Bruton tyrosine kinase), blocking pre-B cell maturation. Physical exam finding: Absence of tonsils and peripheral lymph nodes (due to failure of germinal center formation).

q: At what age do male infants with X-linked Agammaglobulinemia typically present with recurrent bacterial infections, and why?
a: At approximately 6 months of age, coinciding with the decay of transplacentally acquired maternal IgG antibodies.

q: What specific immunophenotypic finding on flow cytometry confirms X-linked Agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's)?
a: Markedly reduced or absent peripheral CD19+ and CD20+ B lymphocytes, along with pan-hypogammaglobulinemia (profound depression of IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE).

q: What classic clinical triad defines Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), and what is its most frequent genetic cause?
a: Triad: Severe failure to thrive, persistent opportunistic infections (fungal, viral, bacterial, Pneumocystis jirovecii), and chronic diarrhea. Most common cause: X-linked recessive IL-2RG gene mutation (common gamma chain deficiency).

q: What metabolic enzyme defect accounts for ~15% of autosomal recessive SCID cases, and what toxicity occurs?
a: Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency. Accumulation of toxic deoxyadenosine (dATP) induces lymphotoxicity, causing depletion of both T and B lymphocytes.

q: What classic radiographic abnormality is present in infants with SCID, and what is the definitive curative treatment?
a: Radiograph: Absence of a thymic shadow (thymic hypoplasia/aplasia). Curative treatment: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).

q: What molecular screening test on dried blood spots enables universal newborn detection of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)?
a: Quantitative PCR detection of T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs); absent or low TREC counts signal severe T-cell lymphopenia.

q: What clinical triad and genetic mutation characterize Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job Syndrome)?
a: Triad: Severe eczema, recurrent "cold" (non-inflammatory) staphylococcal skin abscesses, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections with pneumatocele formation. Genetic mutation: Autosomal dominant STAT3 mutation, impairing Th17 differentiation.

q: What facial, skeletal, and dental features are seen in patients with Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job Syndrome)?
a: Coarse facial features, deep-set eyes, broad nasal bridge, retained primary teeth (double rows of teeth), joint hyperextensibility, and osteopenia with recurrent minimal-trauma fractures.

q: What genetic defect causes Hyper-IgM Syndrome, and what is the cellular mechanism behind the immunoglobulin pattern?
a: Defect: X-linked mutation in CD40 ligand (CD40L / CD154) on helper T cells. Cellular mechanism: Failure of T-cell CD40L to engage B-cell CD40 prevents B-cell class-switch recombination, resulting in elevated/normal IgM with near-absent IgG, IgA, and IgE.

q: Patients with Hyper-IgM Syndrome are uniquely vulnerable to opportunistic infections from which protozoan and fungal pathogens?
a: Protozoan: Cryptosporidium parvum (causing chronic severe watery diarrhea and sclerosing cholangitis). Fungal: Pneumocystis jirovecii (pneumonia).

q: What classic clinical triad defines Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and what characteristic platelet abnormality is seen on peripheral blood smear?
a: Triad: Severe eczema, microthrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections (bacterial, viral, fungal). Platelet feature: Microthrombocytes (significantly decreased platelet volume/size).

q: What gene is mutated in Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and what is the typical serum immunoglobulin profile?
a: Gene: X-linked WAS gene defect (disrupting actin cytoskeleton organization in hematopoietic cells). Serum immunoglobulins: Low to normal IgM, elevated IgA and IgE, with variable IgG.

q: What clinical triad defines Ataxia-Telangiectasia, and what lab biomarker is characteristically elevated?
a: Triad: Progressive cerebellar ataxia (gait instability), oculocutaneous telangiectasias, and immunodeficiency (recurrent sinopulmonary infections). Lab biomarker: Elevated serum α-fetoprotein (AFP).

q: What metabolic/cellular defect causes Ataxia-Telangiectasia, and what major long-term malignancy risk do affected individuals face?
a: Defect: Autosomal recessive mutation in the ATM gene, leading to defective repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Malignancy risk: High incidence of lymphomas and leukemias.

q: What enzymatic defect causes Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), and what modern flow cytometry test confirms the diagnosis?
a: Defect: Mutation in sub-units of NADPH oxidase (most common: X-linked gp91phox), impairing generation of superoxide radicals (O2−). Diagnostic test: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) 123 flow cytometry (demonstrates loss of fluorescence upon oxidation).

q: List 5 major catalase-positive organisms that cause recurrent tissue infections and abscesses in Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).
a:
1. Staphylococcus aureus
2. Aspergillus species
3. Serratia marcescens
4. Burkholderia cepacia
5. Nocardia species.

q: What pathognomonic clinical feature occurs at birth in Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD) Type 1, and what leukocyte abnormality is present?
a: Clinical feature: Delayed umbilical cord separation (>30 days) followed by recurrent necrotic infections without pus formation. Leukocyte abnormality: Marked neutrophilia / leukocytosis during active infection (neutrophils trapped in vasculature).

q: What specific membrane protein is deficient in Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD) Type 1?
a: CD18 (the β2 integrin subunit), which pairs with CD11 to form LFA-1, preventing firm adhesion and extravasation of leukocytes into inflamed tissues.

q: What physical exam triad and microscopic blood smear finding characterize Chédiak-Higashi Syndrome?
a: Exam triad: Partial oculocutaneous albinism, recurrent pyogenic skin/respiratory infections, and progressive peripheral neuropathy. Blood smear: Giant azurophilic granules within neutrophils and lymphocytes (due to LYST lysosomal trafficking gene defect).

q: Patients with inherited deficiencies of terminal complement components (C5–C9) are predisposed to recurrent infections with which specific organism?
a: Recurrent invasive infections with Neisseria species (Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae) due to inability to form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC).

q: Deficiencies in early classical complement components (C1q, C2, C4) strongly predispose patients to developing which autoimmune disorder?
a: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and lupus-like glomerulonephritis, secondary to defective clearance of circulating immune complexes and apoptotic debris.

q: What is Oral Allergy Syndrome (Pollen-Food Allergy Syndrome), and what classic plant-food cross-reactivity is seen with birch tree pollen?
a: IgE-mediated contact urticaria of the lips, tongue, and throat after eating raw fruits/vegetables due to cross-reacting pollen antibodies. Birch pollen cross-reacts with apples, pears, peaches, plums, hazelnuts, and celery.

q: How does Serum Sickness differ pathologically from Serum Sickness-Like Reactions (SSLR), and what antibiotic is the classic cause of SSLR in children?
a: Serum Sickness is a true Type III immune-complex hypersensitivity with complement consumption (low C3/C4). SSLR does not involve immune-complex deposition or complement activation. Classic SSLR trigger: Cefaclor (also amoxicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).

q: What is the classic clinical triad of Serum Sickness, and what is the typical timeframe between antigen exposure and symptom onset?
a: Triad: Fever, urticarial or morbilliform rash, and polyarthralgias/polyarthritis. Onset timeframe: 1 to 2 weeks (7–14 days) after primary drug or foreign antigen exposure.

q: What is the typical incubation period and clinical presentation of DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) syndrome?
a: Incubation: 2 to 8 weeks post-drug exposure. Presentation: High fever, diffuse morbilliform rash progressing to facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia (with atypical lymphocytes), and internal organ damage (most commonly hepatitis).

q: Which high-yield drug classes are most frequently implicated in triggering DRESS syndrome?
a: Allopurinol, aromatic antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine), sulfonamides (Bactrim), and vancomycin.

q: How are Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) categorized based on percentage of Body Surface Area (BSA) epidermal detachment?
a:
SJS: <10% BSA detachment.
SJS/TEN overlap: 10%–30% BSA detachment.
TEN: >30% BSA detachment.

q: What pathognomonic physical exam sign is elicited in SJS/TEN, and what is the primary cause of mortality in these patients?
a: Physical exam sign: Positive Nikolsky sign (epidermal sloughing induced by gentle mechanical pressure). Primary cause of mortality: Sepsis / systemic bacteremia (due to total loss of cutaneous skin barrier) and acute hypovolemic shock.

q: What is the recommended treatment step for Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria that fails standard-dose H1 antihistamines?
a: First step: Increase the dosage of second-generation H1 antihistamines up to 4-fold. If refractory after 4 weeks: Add Omalizumab (anti-IgE monoclonal antibody).

q: Which foods are classic components of Latex-Fruit Syndrome due to cross-reactive IgE epitopes?
a: Avocado, banana, chestnut, and kiwi (the "ABC-K" latex cross-reactive foods).

q: What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of radiocontrast media anaphylactoid reactions, and how are high-risk patients pretreated?
a: Mechanism: Direct, non-IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation driven by hyperosmolality. Prevention: Pretreatment with oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) and H1 antihistamines, plus using low-osmolality contrast agents.

q: What classic clinical triad defines Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD / Samter's Triad)?
a:
1. Asthma
2. Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis
3. Acute broncho-nasal reactions following COX-1 inhibiting NSAIDs or aspirin.

q: What biochemical alteration drives Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD), and what pharmacotherapy targets this pathomechanism?
a: COX-1 inhibition blocks prostaglandin synthesis, shunting arachidonic acid into the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and causing massive overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4). Treatment target: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (Montelukast) or 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor (Zileuton).

q: In which two clinical scenarios is rapid Penicillin desensitization mandatory despite a history of documented IgE-mediated penicillin allergy?
a:
1. Neurosyphilis (or congenital/tertiary syphilis).
2. Syphilis in a pregnant patient.
(Scenarios where penicillin is the only proven bactericidal therapy without acceptable alternatives).

q: What endoscopic and histopathologic findings confirm the diagnosis of Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE)?
a: Endoscopy: Stacked circular rings (trachealization), linear furrows, or microabscesses. Histopathology: ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field (hpf) on distal/proximal esophageal mucosal biopsy after a PPI trial.

q: What pathognomonic somatic gene mutation is present in >90% of cases of Systemic Mastocytosis, and what lab test serves as the principal serum biomarker?
a: Gene mutation: c-KIT D816V mutation (constitutive tyrosine kinase activation). Principal serum biomarker: Elevated baseline serum tryptase (>20 ng/mL).

q: What is Alpha-Gal Syndrome, what vector transmits it, and why is the allergic reaction uniquely delayed?
a: Definition: IgE-mediated allergy against galactose-α-1,3-galactose (carbohydrate on mammalian red meat). Vector: Lone Star tick (Amblyomma americanum) bite. Delay: IgE reaction occurs 3 to 6 hours post-ingestion due to the slow digestion and delayed release of lipid-bound alpha-gal antigens into systemic circulation.

q: What type of hypersensitivity causes Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction, and what diagnostic blood test confirms donor red cell hemolysis?
a: Hypersensitivity: Type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity (pre-existing anti-ABO IgM antibody-mediated intravascular complement lysis). Diagnostic test: Positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT / Direct Coombs test) showing antibody coating of recipient red cells.

q: How can Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI) be clinically differentiated from Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO)?
a:
TRALI: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema from donor anti-HLA antibodies; features normal PCWP, normal BNP, and transient leukopenia, often with hypotension.
TACO: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema from hypervolemia; features elevated BNP (>1.5x baseline), hypertension, neck vein distension, and prompt response to IV loop diuretics.

q: What immunologic mechanisms undergo shift during successful Allergen-Specific Immunotherapy (SCIT/SLIT) to generate persistent clinical tolerance?
a: Shift from Th2 to Th1 immune profile, expansion of regulatory T cells (Treg) secreting IL-10 and TGF-β, and generation of allergen-specific IgG4 blocking antibodies that neutralize allergen before it cross-links IgE on mast cells.
